title: Cloud-Native Design Principles
summary: The mindset shift needed to build software that actually benefits from cloud elasticity — the bridge into containers, Kubernetes, and IaC.

slides.markdown:
"Cloud-native" isn't about *where* your app runs — it's about whether it's built to **exploit** the cloud's elasticity: scale out in seconds, recover from a dead instance without a human, and treat any single machine as disposable.

An app running on cloud VMs but designed like it's 2005 (one big server, in-memory session state, manual failover) is running *on* the cloud, not built *for* it.

slides.subTitle: Beyond the buzzword
slides.markdown:
Cloud-native means an application is designed around the assumptions the cloud actually offers: near-instant provisioning, elastic scale, and frequent, expected component failure. Concretely, that means the app can add or remove instances on demand, survives any single instance dying without a human intervening, and deploys through automated, repeatable pipelines rather than manual steps.

It's a design philosophy, not a specific technology — you can build a cloud-native app on VMs, though containers and orchestration (next topics) make it far easier.

slides.subTitle: The parts that matter most in interviews
slides.markdown:
The 12-factor methodology is a checklist for cloud-native design; the three that come up constantly in interviews are: **config in the environment**, not hardcoded (so the same build runs unchanged in dev, stage, and prod); **stateless processes** with any persistent state pushed to a backing service like a database; and **disposability** — fast startup and graceful shutdown, so instances can be started or killed at any moment without drama.

The others (build/release/run separation, logs as event streams, dev/prod parity) matter in practice but are asked about less often.

slides.subTitle: Why it enables horizontal scaling and fast recovery
slides.markdown:
A **stateless** instance holds no data that would be lost if it disappeared right now — session data, uploaded files, and job progress all live in an external store (a database, cache, or object storage), not in the instance's own memory or disk.

This is what makes horizontal scaling trivial: a load balancer can send any request to any instance, because none of them are "special." It's also what makes fast recovery possible — killing a broken instance and starting a fresh one loses nothing, since nothing important was stored there.

slides.subTitle: Replace, don't patch
slides.markdown:
In **immutable infrastructure**, you never SSH in and modify a running instance — instead you build a new image with the change baked in, and replace the old instance with a new one from that image. The running instance is treated as disposable, never edited in place.

This kills **configuration drift** (no two "identical" servers can quietly diverge from years of one-off manual fixes) and makes rollback trivial — just redeploy the previous image, instead of trying to reverse-engineer what was changed by hand.

slides.subTitle: Assume any component can die at any time
slides.markdown:
Cloud-native design flips the default assumption: instead of engineering to *prevent* failure, you engineer assuming failure **will** happen — an instance, an AZ, or a dependency will go down, on no schedule you control. The system's job is to keep serving traffic anyway: retries with backoff, timeouts on every external call, circuit breakers, and redundant instances across failure domains.

This is why chaos engineering (deliberately killing instances in production to verify the system tolerates it) is a natural extension of cloud-native thinking, not a separate practice.

slides.subTitle: Revisited for cloud elasticity
slides.markdown:
| | Vertical scaling | Horizontal scaling |
|---|---|---|
| How | Bigger instance (more vCPU/RAM) | More instances of the same size |
| Ceiling | Hits a hard limit (the largest instance type) | Effectively unlimited |
| Downtime to scale | Usually requires a restart | None — new instances just join the pool |
| Requires | No app changes | Statelessness, so any instance can serve any request |

**How to decide:** cloud-native systems default to horizontal scaling because it has no ceiling and no downtime — but it only works if the app is stateless enough to spread load across instances freely.

slides.subTitle: Turning a stateful monolith cloud-native
slides.markdown:
A legacy monolith stores user sessions in local memory and writes uploaded files to local disk — so it can only ever run as one instance, and a crash loses in-flight sessions and any file written since the last backup.

Making it cloud-native means: move sessions to a shared cache so any instance can serve any user; move uploads to object storage so the app tier holds nothing irreplaceable; and put the app behind a load balancer with health checks so a dead instance is replaced automatically. None of this requires a rewrite — just relocating state out of the instance.

**Wrong belief:** "We moved our VMs to the cloud, so we're cloud-native now."

**Why it's wrong:** lift-and-shift only changes *where* the servers physically run — the app still holds local state, still can't horizontally scale, and still needs a human to recover from an instance dying. None of the cloud's elasticity actually gets used.

**Correct model:** "cloud-native" describes the application's design (stateless, disposable, horizontally scalable), not its hosting location. A lift-and-shifted app is running *in* the cloud, but it isn't cloud-native until it's redesigned to exploit it.

slides.subTitle: Containers and orchestration
slides.markdown:
Every principle here — statelessness, immutability, designing for failure — is far easier to enforce once your unit of deployment is a **container** rather than a hand-managed VM. A container image bakes in immutability by construction, and an orchestrator like Kubernetes automates exactly the failure-recovery and horizontal-scaling behavior cloud-native design calls for.

That's why the next group of topics moves from these principles straight into containers: they're the practical mechanism that turns cloud-native theory into something you don't have to hand-build yourself.
